question_en: A company recently migrated its application to AWS. The application runs on Amazon EC2 Linux instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The application stores data in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system that uses EFS Standard-Infrequent Access storage. The application indexes the company ' s files, and the index is stored in an Amazon RDS database. The company needs to optimize storage costs with some application and services changes. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Create an Amazon S3 bucket that uses an Intelligent-Tiering lifecycle policy. Copy all files to the S3 bucket. Update the application to use Amazon S3 API to store and retrieve files.
options.B: Deploy Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file shares. Update the application to use CIFS protocol to store and retrieve files.
options.C: Deploy Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system shares. Update the application to use the new mount point to store and retrieve files.
options.D: Create an Amazon S3 bucket that uses S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Copy all files to the S3 bucket. Update the application to use Amazon S3 API to store and retrieve files as standard retrievals.

explanation.full_text: Migrate from EFS to S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Update application to use S3 APIs. Automated cost optimization for varying access patterns.
explanation.why_correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering = automatic storage class transitions based on access. No retrieval fees. Tiers: Frequent ($0.023/GB), Infrequent ($0.0125/GB), Archive Instant ($0.004/GB), Deep Archive ($0.00099/GB). EFS Standard-IA = $0.025/GB vs S3 Intelligent best tier $0.00099/GB. Application change = S3 SDK calls instead of file I/O.

why_wrong.B: FSx for Windows = SMB file server, Active Directory integration. More expensive than S3: $0.013-0.20/GB/month. Unnecessary features (Windows, AD) for Linux application. Doesn't optimize costs—similar or higher than EFS.
why_wrong.C: FSx for OpenZFS = high-performance NFS, snapshots, compression. Cost: $0.15-0.54/GB/month. Good for low-latency workloads but more expensive than S3. Doesn't provide tiering like S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
why_wrong.D: Glacier Flexible Retrieval = manual storage class, not automatic. Retrieval = 3-5 hours, not suitable for application serving files. Would need application redesign to handle async retrieval. S3 API changes required anyway—Intelligent-Tiering better.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Optimize storage costs' + 'unpredictable access' = S3 Intelligent-Tiering. EFS = shared file system for EC2. FSx = managed file servers (Windows/Lustre/NetApp/OpenZFS). S3 = object storage, lowest cost at scale. File to object = application changes required.
memorize: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: automatic tiering, $0.0025/1K objects monitoring

question_en: An ecommerce company is redesigning a web application to run on the AWS Cloud. The application needs to store static website content and must use a Microsoft SQL Server database to store customer data. The company needs to deploy the application in a resilient way across multiple Availability Zones. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store static content. Deploy an Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server DB instance for the database.
options.B: Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store static content. Create an Amazon RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ deployment for the database.
options.C: Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach volume to store static content. Deploy an Amazon RDS for SQL Server DB instance for the database.
options.D: Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach volume to store static content. Deploy SQL Server on two Amazon EC2 instances in separate Availability Zones.

explanation.why_correct: S3 provides durable, highly available static content storage with 99.999999999% durability. RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ maintains standby replica in different AZ with automatic failover. Both services natively support multi-AZ resilience with minimal manual intervention.

why_wrong.A: RDS Custom requires OS-level management, increasing operational overhead vs. standard RDS Multi-AZ for simple HA requirement.
why_wrong.C: EBS Multi-Attach not designed for static website content—limited functionality, wrong tool. Lacks object storage semantics.
why_wrong.D: EBS Multi-Attach wrong for static content. Self-managed SQL Server on EC2 requires manual clustering, patching, backup configuration—high operational overhead.

explanation.exam_tips: For static website content: S3 (not EBS). For SQL Server Multi-AZ HA: RDS Multi-AZ (not RDS Custom or EC2). RDS Custom is for deep OS/DB customization, not basic HA.
explanation.memorize: Multi-AZ web app = S3 (static) + RDS Multi-AZ (database resilience)

question_en: A company runs a multi-tier application on premises by using virtual machines (VMs). The application tiers communicate asynchronously through third-party middleware that guarantees exactly-once delivery. The company is planning to migrate the application to AWS and needs to replace the middleware solution. The solution must provide exactly-once delivery for messages from the application. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements with the LEAST infrastructure management? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Use AWS Lambda functions to provide compute layers in the architecture.
options.B: Use Amazon EC2 instances to provide compute layers in the architecture.
options.C: Use Amazon SNS as a messaging component between the compute layers.
options.D: Use Amazon SQS FIFO queues as a messaging component between the compute layers.
options.E: Run containers on Amazon EKS to provide compute layers in the architecture.

explanation.why_correct: SQS FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once delivery with ordered processing. Lambda provides fully managed compute without infrastructure management (no VMs, OS, or clusters). Perfect for asynchronous multi-tier communication.

why_wrong.B: EC2 instances require managing provisioning, patching, scaling, and availability—violating least management requirement.
why_wrong.C: Amazon SNS provides pub/sub but lacks exactly-once delivery guarantees required for this migration.
why_wrong.E: Amazon EKS introduces Kubernetes management overhead, not the lowest-management option.

explanation.exam_tips: For exactly-once message delivery: use SQS FIFO (not SNS). For least infrastructure management: Lambda (not EC2 or EKS). FIFO guarantees order + exactly-once.
explanation.memorize: Exactly-once + least management = SQS FIFO + Lambda

question_en: A company needs a solution to process customer orders from a global ecommerce platform. The solution must automatically start processing new orders immediately and must maintain a history of all order processing attempts. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes an AWS Lambda function once every minute to check for new orders. Configure the Lambda function to process orders and store results in Amazon Aurora.
options.B: Create an Amazon EventBridge event pattern that monitors the ecommerce platform ' s order events. Configure an EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function when the platform receives a new order. Configure the function to store the results in Amazon DynamoDB.
options.C: Use an Amazon EC2 instance to poll the ecommerce platform for new orders. Configure the instance to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process new orders. Configure the function to log results to Amazon CloudWatch.
options.D: Use an Amazon SQS queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function when the platform receives a new order. Configure the function to process batches of orders and to store results in an Amazon EFS file system.

explanation.full_text: EventBridge event-driven pattern invokes Lambda immediately when order arrives. Lambda processes and stores in DynamoDB. Most cost-effective serverless solution.
explanation.why_correct: EventBridge = monitors ecommerce platform events in real-time. Lambda invoked only on actual orders—no polling waste. DynamoDB = NoSQL, scales automatically, stores processing history with low latency. Fully serverless = no idle costs, auto-scales to global traffic.

why_wrong.A: Lambda every minute polling = 1,440 invocations/day even with zero orders. Polling introduces latency (up to 60s delay). Aurora = relational DB overkill and more expensive than DynamoDB for event logs.
why_wrong.C: EC2 polling = 24/7 instance costs (~$180/mo minimum t3.small). Manual scaling needed. CloudWatch Logs = not queryable database, lacks structured storage for history.
why_wrong.D: SQS doesn't 'invoke' Lambda—Lambda polls SQS (different model). EFS = file storage not suited for structured order processing history. More expensive than DynamoDB for this use case.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Immediately' + 'event-driven' + 'history' = EventBridge + Lambda + DynamoDB. Polling (cron, EC2 checking) = anti-pattern for event-driven. DynamoDB = event/activity logging. Aurora = complex transactional queries. CloudWatch Logs = monitoring, not app database.
memorize: DynamoDB: 25GB storage free, 25 WCU/25 RCU free tier
Polling vs push: push = immediate, polling = delay + waste
Event-driven: EventBridge, SNS, SQS; avoid cron for real-time

question_en: A company runs its applications on both Amazon EKS clusters and on-premises Kubernetes clusters. The company wants to view all clusters and workloads from a central location. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.B: Use Amazon EKS Connector to register and connect all Kubernetes clusters.
options.C: Use AWS Systems Manager to collect and view the cluster information.
options.D: Use Amazon EKS Anywhere as the primary cluster to view the other clusters with native Kubernetes commands.

explanation.why_correct: EKS Connector registers external Kubernetes clusters (on-prem or other clouds) to AWS, enabling centralized visibility in EKS console. Displays clusters and workloads from multiple locations with minimal operational overhead. Purpose-built for hybrid Kubernetes management.

why_wrong.A: CloudWatch Container Insights provides metrics/logs but doesn't centrally register and display cluster inventory across environments.
why_wrong.C: Systems Manager doesn't provide Kubernetes cluster centralized management or workload visibility.
why_wrong.D: EKS Anywhere runs Kubernetes on-prem but isn't designed for centralized viewing of existing clusters—requires migration.

explanation.exam_tips: For hybrid Kubernetes visibility (EKS + on-prem): use EKS Connector. Don't confuse with Container Insights (monitoring only) or EKS Anywhere (run K8s on-prem).
explanation.memorize: Centralized K8s view (EKS + on-prem) = EKS Connector

question_en: A company hosts dozens of multi-tier applications on AWS. The presentation layer and logic layer are Amazon EC2 Linux instances that use Amazon EBS volumes. The company needs a solution to ensure that operating system vulnerabilities are not introduced to the EC2 instances when the company deploys new features. The company uses custom AMIs to deploy EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The solution must scale to handle all applications that the company hosts. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon Inspector to patch operating system vulnerabilities. Invoke Amazon Inspector when a new AMI is deployed.
options.B: Use AWS Backup to back up the EBS volume of each updated instance. Use the EBS backup volumes to create new AMIs. Use the existing Auto Scaling group to deploy the new AMIs.
options.C: Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to patch operating system vulnerabilities in the custom AMIs.
options.D: Use EC2 Image Builder to create new AMIs when the company deploys new features. Include the update-linux component in the build components of the new AMIs. Use the existing Auto Scaling group to deploy the new AMIs.

explanation.why_correct: EC2 Image Builder automates AMI creation with patching, testing, and hardening. Update-linux component applies OS security patches during image build. Creates golden AMIs preventing vulnerabilities at deployment time. Scales across applications via reusable pipelines with minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: Inspector identifies vulnerabilities but doesn't patch AMIs. Cannot be invoked to patch images during creation.
why_wrong.B: AWS Backup backs up data, doesn't patch or create AMIs. Wrong tool for vulnerability management.
why_wrong.C: Patch Manager patches running instances, not base AMIs. Doesn't prevent vulnerabilities in new deployments.

explanation.exam_tips: For patched AMI creation at scale: EC2 Image Builder with update-linux component. Inspector scans (doesn't patch), Patch Manager patches live instances (not AMIs).
explanation.memorize: Patched golden AMIs at scale = EC2 Image Builder + update-linux component

question_en: A company has developed an API using an Amazon API Gateway REST API and AWS Lambda functions. The API serves static and dynamic content to users worldwide. The company wants to decrease the latency of transferring content for API requests. Options:

options.A: Deploy the REST API as an edge-optimized API endpoint. Enable caching. Enable content encoding in the API definition to compress the application data in transit.
options.B: Deploy the REST API as a Regional API endpoint. Enable caching. Enable content encoding in the API definition to compress the application data in transit.
options.C: Deploy the REST API as an edge-optimized API endpoint. Enable caching. Configure reserved concurrency for the Lambda functions.
options.D: Deploy the REST API as a Regional API endpoint. Enable caching. Configure reserved concurrency for the Lambda functions.

explanation.why_correct: Edge-optimized API Gateway uses CloudFront edge locations globally. Caching reduces latency. Content encoding compresses data, reducing transfer time.

why_wrong.B: Regional API Gateway serves single region, no global edge optimization.
why_wrong.C: Reserved concurrency ensures capacity, doesn't reduce content transfer latency.
why_wrong.D: Regional API + reserved concurrency doesn't optimize global latency.

explanation.exam_tips: Edge-optimized = CloudFront edge locations. Regional = single region. Caching + compression = reduce latency.
explanation.memorize: Edge-optimized API + caching + compression = minimize global latency.
